EPISODE_NARRATIVE: 60 to 65 mph winds blew down numerous trees and power lines. A house and nearby outbuilding were heavily damaged as well.

A strong coastal low pressure system moved northeast into southeastern Massachusetts from south of Long Island and brought high winds to many parts of southeastern Massachusetts, including Cape Cod and the Islands.  There were even a few gusts to hurricane force.  The strong winds blew from the east and southeast and gusts frequently reached 50 to 65 mph across much of the state...from Middlesex and Norfolk Counties east and southeast. Peak wind gusts of 81 mph were recorded both at Cuttyhunk Island west of Martha's Vineyard and atop Blue Hill in Milton.  Some of the other highest wind gusts reported included: 79 mph at the New Bedford Hurricane Barrier; 77 mph at Dennis; 73 mph at Hyannis; 71 mph at Marstons Mills (Falmouth); and 60 mph at Chatham.  Numerous trees and tree limbs were blown down, knocking out electrical power.  Outages affected up to 32,000 electric customers statewide, including 12,000 in southeastern Massachusetts and 20,000 in the Merrimack Valley.  There were scattered reports of trees falling onto homes causing scattered property damage.Heavy rainfall occurred, with the maximum totals of 2.0 to 3.6 inches reported from the south coast across Cape Cod and the Islands.  Heavy rain also fell across the rest of the state with 1.5 to more than 3.0 inches in less than 12 hours.  In Hampshire County, Worthington reported a total of 3.06 inches.    Lowell had 2.24 inches and Worcester had 2.22 inches.   In New Bedford, along the south coast, 3.47 inches was reported.  Major urban street flooding occurred in Dartmouth, New Bedford, and Acushnet.  There were many reports of flooding...and not just in poor drainage areas.  There were reports of minor shore road flooding along the south coast and along Martha's Vineyard's shores at normally vulnerable locations.  Thirteen crewmen had to be rescued from a sinking fishing vessel off of Gloucester.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: 8 inches of new snow at the higher elevations of the Southern Sierra Nevada.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving nor'easter caused strong winds, beach erosion and widespread, but minor, tidal flooding from mid-day on the 7th through the afternoon on the 8th.  The low pressure system formed near Cape Hatteras on the morning of the 7th and moved slowly north as the surface low was captured by a closed low at higher levels of the atmosphere.  On the morning of the 8th,  it was located about 80 miles east of Wallops Island Virginia and on the morning of the 9th,  it was near Cape May City.  That morning a second low pressure system was located near Cape Cod Massachusetts and the two merged into one and was located just south of Nova Scotia by the morning of the 10th.  The low came close enough to the New Jersey shore by the morning of the 9th to cause the onshore winds and consequently the tidal flooding to diminish.The several tide cycle pounding cause beach erosion along the New Jersey Coast and it became severe in a few locations.  In Cape May County, in Sea Isle City, severe erosion occurred from 89th through 93rd Streets and the ocean came within 15 feet of the Tiburon Shores Condominiums.  The surf removed dunes and steps in that area.  In Ocean County, in Harvey Cedars, the pounding surf scoured a six foot cliff north of Bergen Avenue.  In Brant Beach, waves crashed close to the dunes on  41st Street.  In Monmouth County, the surf removed about 50 to 100 feet of beach in Manasquan and created a four foot cliff in Spring Lake. The persistent onshore flow raised tidal departures to 3.0 to 3.5 feet above normal and around 2.5 feet above normal at times of high tide from mid-day on the 7th (Friday) through the afternoon on the 8th (Saturday).  This caused widespread, but minor,  tidal flooding from the mid-day high tide on the 7th through the afternoon on the 8th.   The highest tides reported were 6.6 feet above mean low water in Atlantic City, 6.9 feet above mean low water in Sandy Hook and 7.4 feet above mean low water in Cape May City.  In Monmouth County, tidal flooding was reported along the Shrewsbury River in Rumson and Sea Bright.  In Ocean County, in Beach Haven, minor tidal flooding occurred along Bay Avenue and minor flooding was also reported in Barnegat.  In Atlantic County, in Absecon, the intersection of  U.S. Route 9 and Shore Road were closed for several hours the evening of the 7th.  Some bayside blocks in southern Atlantic City were flooded.  In Cape May County, tidal flooding forced the closure of several blocks in Ocean City and Wildwood. Strong gusty winds buffeted the region from the morning of the 7th through the afternoon of the 8th.  The strongest gusts were reported during the afternoon and evening of the 7th.  Peak gusts included 59 mph in Williamstown (Gloucester County), 56 mph in Seaside Park and Harvey Cedars (both Ocean County), 47 mph at the Marina in Atlantic City, 45 mph in Belmar and 44 mph in Wildwood.  In Ocean County, the strong winds caused power outages to about 5,000 homes in Stafford Township and ripped away beach fencing in Beach Haven.  During the same storm, a ship reported a severe thunderstorm that produced wind gusts to 86 mph at 10 p.m. EST on the 8th about 100 nautical miles east of Cape May County.

A "southeaster" brought strong east to southeast winds to coastal eastern Massachusetts with wind gusts to 40 to 55 mph. In New Bedford, a tree fell on a house and car.  In Dartmouth, a staging was toppled at the University of Massachusetts.  At least five boats washed ashore and countless others lost rudders at Mattapoisett Harbor.  The town wharf was under about six inches of water at high tide.  The harbormaster rated this storm as one of the top five bad storms during recent years.  Minor coastal flooding was reported at many points along south facing coastlines of southeastern Massachusetts, with tides one to two feet above normal.  The strong winds in the Boston area reached sustained speeds of 30 mph at Deer Island in Boston Harbor.  A peak gust to 51 mph was recorded from the east-southeast at the Blue Hill Observatory in Milton at 11:08 AM.  Heavy rain accompanied the winds.  Very heavy rain fell on Martha's Vineyard where the storm total was 3.8 inches.  This was the same storm system that hit Atlantic City, NJ with a deluge of around 14 inches of rainfall.

The wind died down during the evening. The strong winds blew down numerous tree limbs and a few large trees throughout northern Illinois. The falling limbs knocked out power to over 40,000 customers. Flights were delayed at O'Hare Airport. A tree fell on a police car in Barrington Hills, but the officer in the car was not injured. The high winds also fanned brush and grass fires in Livingston, Ford and Iroquois Counties.

On November 30, light freezing rain spread across eastern New York from south to north during the early morning hours.  The freezing rain made the morning commute treacherous in most areas.  Many accidents occurred during the morning and early afternoon which resulted in several road closures.  Interstate 88 was closed from Rotterdam in Schenectady County through its entire length in Schoharie County.  The closure lasted only one hour during the morning but portions were closed again during the late afternoon to clear several accidents.  In Fulton County, state highway 29 was closed from the Village of Dolgeville to Oppenheim.  The Taconic State Parkway in Dutchess and Columbia Counties, remained opened but was hazardous.  The light freezing rain stopped across the southern areas by noontime but continued from the Mohawk Valley north through mid afternoon.  In the southern Adirondacks and upper Hudson Valley the freezing rain changed to light snow during the early evening.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall of 10 to 24 inches accompanied by 50 to 60 mph winds produced widespread blizzard conditions with near zero visibility and wind chills to 20 degrees below zero. It was the largest one day snowfall on record at the Goodland NWS office with 19.3 inches. Other snowfall amounts were St. Francis 11 inches, Bird City 19, McDonald 16, Atwood 14, Oberlin 17, Norcatur 24, Dresden 17, Lenora 22, Norton 12, Densmore 21, Colby 20, Rexford 11, Mingo 18, Hoxie 18, Morland 16, St. Peter 18, Hill City 12, Sharon Springs 19, Oakley 12, Winona 20, Gove 9, Grainfield 8, Quinter 12, Tribune 22, Leoti 13. Drifts 6 to 12 feet were common. An estimated 6200 head of cattle were killed.  The Air National Guard air lifted hay to surviving range cattle after the storm.  Up to 25 percent of the remaining fall crops were damaged by the snow and wind. Roads were closed and motorists stranded. At least one person suffered severe frostbite and mild hypothermia after becoming stranded for over 12 hours when his snowmobile quit.  All activities were cancelled or postponed. Schools were closed for 1 to 2 days afterwards.  The roof on the Student Union Building at Northwest Kansas Technical School in Goodland collapsed with $250,000 damage. The weight of the snow also damaged carports and awnings. Snowdrifts 1 to 2 feet high were even found in attics near vents due to wind blown snow. These inside drifts melted and subsequently caused ceiling, wall, and insulation damage in many homes.

A strong cold front moving across the Great Lakes region collided with warm, moist, and unstable air across the southern Lower Peninsula on Friday afternoon, September 19, 1997. A cold front moved across western Lower Michigan during the early morning hours of November 12th, resulting in a lake-enhanced snow event which began late evening, Tuesday, November 11th. In general, 1 to 5 inches of snow fell across western and southern Lower Michigan, with 3 to 5 inch amounts confined to Lake, Ottawa, Kent, Allegan, Barry, Eaton, Ingham, and Kalamazoo Counties. The snow-covered and icy roads caught many overnight and early morning motorists by surprise. Slippery conditions are believed to have contributed to a seven-car pile-up on the northbound span of the U.S. 31 drawbridge late Tuesday night in Grand Haven. Two injuries were reported. This resulted in extremely icy conditions and an unusually high number of minor accidents, which included many slide-offs into ditches. On November 30, light freezing rain spread across eastern New York from south to north during the early morning hours.  The freezing rain made the morning commute treacherous in most areas.  Many accidents occurred during the morning and early afternoon which resulted in several road closures.  Interstate 88 was closed from Rotterdam in Schenectady County through its entire length in Schoharie County.  The closure lasted only one hour during the morning but portions were closed again during the late afternoon to clear several accidents.  In Fulton County, state highway 29 was closed from the Village of Dolgeville to Oppenheim.  The Taconic State Parkway in Dutchess and Columbia Counties, remained opened but was hazardous.  The light freezing rain stopped across the southern areas by noontime but continued from the Mohawk Valley north through mid afternoon.  In the southern Adirondacks and upper Hudson Valley the freezing rain changed to light snow during the early evening.

Unseasonably dry weather with below normal rainfall, which became worse during the summer months, forced the Delaware River Basin Commission to declare a drought warning on October 27th.  The commission urged the 7 million residents within the basin's 13,539 square mile area to voluntarily conserve water.  Water levels in the New York City Reservoirs, which are in the headwaters of the Delaware River, fell below 40 percent of capacity in late October.  Also, the salt line in the Delaware River, was located near Bridgeport in Gloucester County, approximately four miles farther north than it should have been for late October.  The yearly precipitation totals on a county weighted average were below normal in all of New Jersey except for Atlantic, Cape May and Cumberland Counties.  Precipitation deficits through October 31st averaged around 5 inches in the other counties.  The greatest deficits were in Salem (-7.2 inches), Morris (-7.1 inches) and Somerset (-6.0 inches) Counties.  In the latter three counties, this was about 80 percent of the normal precipitation.  Because a large number of New Jersey farms have irrigation capabilities, agricultural losses from the drought were not as severe as they were in Maryland and Pennsylvania.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong coastal low pressure system moved northeast into southeastern Massachusetts from south of Long Island and brought high winds to many parts of southeastern Massachusetts, including Cape Cod and the Islands.  There were even a few gusts to hurricane force.  The strong winds blew from the east and southeast and gusts frequently reached 50 to 65 mph across much of the state...from Middlesex and Norfolk Counties east and southeast. Peak wind gusts of 81 mph were recorded both at Cuttyhunk Island west of Martha's Vineyard and atop Blue Hill in Milton.  Some of the other highest wind gusts reported included: 79 mph at the New Bedford Hurricane Barrier; 77 mph at Dennis; 73 mph at Hyannis; 71 mph at Marstons Mills (Falmouth); and 60 mph at Chatham.  Numerous trees and tree limbs were blown down, knocking out electrical power.  Outages affected up to 32,000 electric customers statewide, including 12,000 in southeastern Massachusetts and 20,000 in the Merrimack Valley.  There were scattered reports of trees falling onto homes causing scattered property damage.Heavy rainfall occurred, with the maximum totals of 2.0 to 3.6 inches reported from the south coast across Cape Cod and the Islands.  Heavy rain also fell across the rest of the state with 1.5 to more than 3.0 inches in less than 12 hours.  In Hampshire County, Worthington reported a total of 3.06 inches.    Lowell had 2.24 inches and Worcester had 2.22 inches.   In New Bedford, along the south coast, 3.47 inches was reported.  Major urban street flooding occurred in Dartmouth, New Bedford, and Acushnet.  There were many reports of flooding...and not just in poor drainage areas.  There were reports of minor shore road flooding along the south coast and along Martha's Vineyard's shores at normally vulnerable locations.  Thirteen crewmen had to be rescued from a sinking fishing vessel off of Gloucester.

On Saturday, August 16, 1997, a cold front moved slowly south across Michigan's Lower Peninsula. One low pressure wave moved along the front early that morning, resulting in severe thunderstorm development over south central Lower Michigan. Later that afternoon, with very humid and unstable air in place across far southern Lower Michigan, another frontal wave caused severe thunderstorm development along the southern 2 tier of counties across southern Michigan. The thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall amounts of 2 to 5 inches in the counties bordering northern Indiana and northern Ohio, along with isolated reports of wind damage from 60 mph thunderstorm wind gusts. One thunderstorm produced golfball-sized hail in Edwardsburg in Cass County on Saturday afternoon. Local utility companies reported approximately 55,000 power outages during the afternoon and evening across far southern Michigan, most a result of lightning strikes, but some due to downed trees and utility poles.

The  main rain / snow line set up from near Salisbury northeast to Greensboro and extended northeast to the North Carolina / Virginia border, just west of Roxboro. Snow fell to the west of this line, while rain fell to the east.   Along the narrow transition zone from near Salisbury  northeast  to Roxboro,  a mixture of rain and snow fell, occasionally mixed with sleet. Accumulations of snow were heaviest in the city of Winston-Salem and  points west and north of the city.  Totals  there  were from 6 to 8 inches, with 4 to 6 inches of snow in Davidson and  Guilford counties, including the cities of Lexington and Greensboro.  Near the snow to rain transition line...snow accumulations were limited to 1 to 3 inches in a zone from Albemarle in Stanly county northeast through Randolph county including Asheboro and into Alamance and Person counties. Burlington and Roxboro reported around 2 inches of snow. Hundreds of traffic accidents were reported in Davidson, Forsyth, Guilford, Randolph, and Alamance counties. Power outages were also heaviest in Forsyth county.

Record cold accompanied the snow as temperatures dropped to the single digits the morning of the 26th.

A coastal storm or nor'easter developed along the South Carolina coast the morning of the 13th and moved slowly northeast and was about 75 miles east of Salisbury Maryland at 7 a.m. EST on the 14th.  The low pressure system then accelerated and was well southeast of Nova Scotia on the morning of the 15th.  Preceding this low pressure system was an unseasonably cold and dry air mass.  This factor coupled with the northeast flow around the coastal low and the presence of a new and fresh supply of cold air supplied by another high pressure system in nearby Canada kept temperatures near the ground at or below the freezing mark.  Thus precipitation fell as mainly freezing rain.  The freezing rain caused power outages and contributed to three fatalities involving motor vehicles.Precipitation started during the late evening on the 13th and lasted about 24 hours ending as a period of light snow across much of the area, especially in the Poconos where 1 to 3 inches accumulated on top of the ice.  In Upper Bucks County,  freezing rain fell during the morning of the 14th, before most locations rose above the freezing mark.  Some pockets of freezing formed again that evening before the precipitation ended.  The ground was still relatively warm and ice accrued mainly on power lines, tree limbs, bridges and overpasses.  A 38 year-old Allentown woman was killed at 140 a.m. EST on the 14th when she lost control of her car.  At 9 p.m. EST on the 14th a 51-year-old man and his 17-year-old son were killed when they lost control of their car on the Northeast Extension of the Pennsylvania Turnpike in Kidder Township (Carbon County) and were broadsided by a tractor trailer.  The Pennsylvania State Police division in the Poconos advised against nonessential travel because of numerous reports of fender benders and vehicles sliding off roadways.As the freezing rain continued to accrue on trees and power lines (about one-half to three-quarters of an inch of ice accrued on most surfaces), they started to come down.  Pennsylvania Power and Light reported about 50,000 homes and businesses lost power in their northeast Pennsylvania service area.  It took about 24 hours to bring the last 5,000 customers back on line.  In Lehigh County, there were numerous outages on the east and south side of Allentown and also in South Whitehall Township.  The greatest accretion of ice occurred in the northeast part of the county.  In Northampton County numerous outages were reported in Bethlehem and three vehicles were damaged by fallen limbs.  Few neighborhoods were spared tree damage.  The most ice though accrued in the northwest part of the county around Danielsville.  In Berks County, the greatest ice accretion and most of the fallen limbs were reported from Oley northeast to the Blue Mountains.

This factor coupled with the northeast flow around the coastal low and the presence of a new and fresh supply of cold air supplied by another high pressure system in nearby Canada kept temperatures near the ground at or below the freezing mark.  Thus precipitation fell as mainly freezing rain.  The freezing rain caused power outages and contributed to three fatalities involving motor vehicles.Precipitation started during the late evening on the 13th and lasted about 24 hours ending as a period of light snow across much of the area, especially in the Poconos where 1 to 3 inches accumulated on top of the ice.  In Upper Bucks County,  freezing rain fell during the morning of the 14th, before most locations rose above the freezing mark.  Some pockets of freezing formed again that evening before the precipitation ended.  The ground was still relatively warm and ice accrued mainly on power lines, tree limbs, bridges and overpasses.  A 38 year-old Allentown woman was killed at 140 a.m. EST on the 14th when she lost control of her car.  At 9 p.m. EST on the 14th a 51-year-old man and his 17-year-old son were killed when they lost control of their car on the Northeast Extension of the Pennsylvania Turnpike in Kidder Township (Carbon County) and were broadsided by a tractor trailer.  The Pennsylvania State Police division in the Poconos advised against nonessential travel because of numerous reports of fender benders and vehicles sliding off roadways.As the freezing rain continued to accrue on trees and power lines (about one-half to three-quarters of an inch of ice accrued on most surfaces), they started to come down.  Pennsylvania Power and Light reported about 50,000 homes and businesses lost power in their northeast Pennsylvania service area.  It took about 24 hours to bring the last 5,000 customers back on line.  In Lehigh County, there were numerous outages on the east and south side of Allentown and also in South Whitehall Township.  The greatest accretion of ice occurred in the northeast part of the county.  In Northampton County numerous outages were reported in Bethlehem and three vehicles were damaged by fallen limbs.  Few neighborhoods were spared tree damage.  The most ice though accrued in the northwest part of the county around Danielsville.  In Berks County, the greatest ice accretion and most of the fallen limbs were reported from Oley northeast to the Blue Mountains.

The ice brought down tree limbs and power lines and caused power outages to 2,000 customers across Northwest New Jersey.  A downed tree in Randolph Township (Morris County) caused the greatest concentration of outages in one area.   The freezing rain contributed to numerous accidents across Northwest New Jersey.  In Newton (Sussex County) alone twice vehicles were involved in head-on collisions after they slid into oncoming traffic.  In Morris County, a Morris Township bus driver fractured both legs after the bus slid off a driveway into a tree.  Two children were also injured.  In Denville, a car slid into a guide wire, while in Parsippany, a van flipped onto its roof.

With a strong high pressure system extending from north of New England southwest across the Great Lakes, a low pressure system formed off the Southeast Coast during Thursday, November 6th.  The low slowly intensified as it moved very slowly north off the Mid-Atlantic Coast Friday and Saturday.  It did not pass north of the area until Sunday, November 9th.The heaviest rain fell during Saturday morning and afternoon on November 8th.  Generally 1 to 2 inches of rain fell across the area.  However, specific amounts ranged from 0.66 inches at Bridgehampton (Suffolk County) to 2.65 inches at Montgomery (Orange County). Minor flooding of low-lying poor drainage areas occurred where leafs clogged drains.Northeast gales developed over the coastal waters after 7 am Friday, November 7th and lasted until around 8 am on Saturday, November 8th.  Seas peaked at 12 to 15 feet from 10 am on Friday through 10 am on Saturday.Northeast winds gusted from 30 to 40 mph.  The highest peak gust was 44 mph at LaGuardia Airport on Friday, November 7th and 47 mph on Saturday, November 8th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Deep southerly flow of modified tropical air produce two small spin-up tornadoes in the western Virginia piedmont  during the late afternoon.  The first touchdown occurred near Orange.  A witness at the Piedmont Research Center saw a funnel cloud briefly touch down into a field, causing a debris swirl (most likely dirt and grass).  The tornado  lifted as quickly as it touched down, near federal highway 15.  A survey team noted only a swirling effect flattened grass in the field.A stronger twister touched down about an hour later near Radiant.  The twister, witnessed by several onlookers, first moved across a farm field, causing minor damage to a building and an adjacent satellite dish before flipping an empty livestock truck.  The truck, which landed on hay bales, was undamaged.  The storm moved through a wooded area, then moved into a residential area where a dozen trees were uprooted or snapped.  Minor damage was sustained to the houses.  The twister then dissipated.  Estimated winds ranged from 70 to 80 mph.

Gradient winds caused widespread damage to trees and property in Iowa and Illinois.  Over 65,000 power customers were without power for several days due to downed power lines. A large cottonwood tree fell on a home in Camanche causing serious structural damage.  The winds slowed river operations at Lock and Dam 13 near Fulton IL as some boaters were afraid to leave the safety of the narrow channel and enter the wide open upstream pool where winds might capsize their boats.

A fast-moving and rapidly deepening low pressure system raced from the South Carolina coast to east of New Jersey in eight hours.  An area of moderate to occasionally heavy snow developed over western North Carolina during the morning and raced through eastern West Virginia during the afternoon and early evening.  Across the eastern panhandle, accumulations ranged from 5 to 9 inches. Heavier snow fell in the Potomac Highlands, with totals ranging from 9 to 13 inches.  Higher mountainous terrain received up to 15 inches.  Additional light snow continued over the far western portion of Grant, Mineral, and Pendleton Cos (WVZ048>049-054) into New Year's Eve.Blowing and drifting snow on the 30th created some travel headaches, but problems were minimal.  However, a notable accident occurred outside of Martinsburg (WVZ052) when a tractor-trailer flipped along Interstate 81.  The storm occurred during a period of low traffic volume between the Christmas and New Year's holidays.

A strong coastal low pressure system moved northeast into southeastern Massachusetts from south of Long Island and brought strong east to southeast winds to the central and south portion of Rhode Island.  A few gusts to hurricane force occurred along the south coast with Point Judith reporting 79 mph.  Scattered power outages were reported, especially near the south coast.  Many boats were reported blown off their moorings in North Kingstown, where minor coastal flooding occurred.  Water was reported two feet over the sea wall in isolated locations.  Heavy rain fell with this storm.  A few amounts included:  Clayville, 3.26 inches; Woonsocket, 2.54 inches; and Newport, 2.00 inches.

A moist northwest flow resulted in 4 to 8 inches of new snow over many mountain areas of western Colorado, and 3 to 5 inches in some northwest valleys.  Heavier snowfall reports included 14 inches at Columbine, 13 inches at Climax, and 10 inches at Vail Ski Area.

A cold front moved across western Lower Michigan during the early morning hours of November 12th, resulting in a lake-enhanced snow event which began late evening, Tuesday, November 11th. In general, 1 to 5 inches of snow fell across western and southern Lower Michigan, with 3 to 5 inch amounts confined to Lake, Ottawa, Kent, Allegan, Barry, Eaton, Ingham, and Kalamazoo Counties. The snow-covered and icy roads caught many overnight and early morning motorists by surprise. Slippery conditions are believed to have contributed to a seven-car pile-up on the northbound span of the U.S. 31 drawbridge late Tuesday night in Grand Haven. Two injuries were reported. The snow initially melted on road surfaces overnight, then froze early Wednesday morning as temperatures fell below freezing. This resulted in extremely icy conditions and an unusually high number of minor accidents, which included many slide-offs into ditches. Accidents with injuries were reported in Battle Creek, St. Joseph and Cass Counties, Hillsdale County (a rollover accident), and  Branch, Mecosta, Osceola, and Newaygo Counties. Snow reports included 5.0 inches in Grandville, 4.8 inches at the National Weather Service Office in southeast Grand Rapids, 4.5 inches in Hudsonville, 3.6-4.0 inches in Allegan, 3.2 inches in Hastings, 3.0 inches in Oshtemo, 3.0 inches in East Lansing, and 1.5 inches in Battle Creek.

Slowly developing low pressure off the southeast U.S. coast generated a prolonged period of moderate to heavy rains over much of northern Virginia for most of the day.  Rainfall averaging 2 to 4 inches, with localized totals between 4 and 6 inches, caused minor flooding of creeks and small streams.  Dozens of secondary roads were closed in the area, most due to swollen creeks but others from high standing water.  Nine school districts closed early, including the following:  Rockingham, Shenandoah, Frederick, Page, Warren, Clarke, Rappahannock, Culpeper, and Fauquier Cos.  One good example of high water occurred in southeast Fauquier Co, where Town Creek was 1.5 feet out of its banks.Some areas had many more roads closed than others.   Tops on the list were Culpeper Co with 25 closures; Frederick Co with 20, Shenandoah Co with 21, and Warren Co with 15.  Only one major highway was reported closed; federal highway 211 near local route 658 in eastern Page Co.  Though no deaths or injuries were noted, one automobile was washed away, and its four occupants rescued, after encountering high water along River Road in southern Stafford Co near Fredericksburg.Rain tapered off during the late afternoon, and streams and creeks receded quickly during the evening.
The monthly average temperature was 3 to 6 degrees below normal,  with the coldest readings during the 2nd and 3rd weeks.  It was the third consecutive November that was unusually cold.

A very wet snow fell in all of North Central, Northeast and East Central Kansas.  The precipitation was mostly snow from the onset in North Central Kansas.  In East Central and most of Northeast Kansas however heavy rain turned to heavy snow with snowfall rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour shortly after the changeover occurred.  Total accumulations were held down due to soaked ground and temperatures slightly above freezing.  The greatest snowfall of 4 to 6 inches fell generally north of Interstate 70.  Some specific amounts include Blaine and Concordia 6 inches, Circleville and Munden 5 inches,  Seneca 4 to 6 inches, Hiawatha, Marysville and Manhattan 4 inches.  Several vehicle accidents resulted with one of them fatal.  A motorist lost control on northbound US Highway 59 four miles north of Ottawa in Franklin County and was hit on the passenger side by a suburban vehicle as he slid into the opposing lane.  The motorist was killed while the driver of the suburban vehicle suffered minor injuries.

An upper level low pressure system combined with upslope northerly winds at the surface to produce widespread snow across the southeast mountains and adjoining plains starting the morning of the 24th and lasting into Christmas morning.  Storm totals ranged from 4 to 9 inches in and around the Wet Mountains.  However, 12 inches of snow fell in Cuchara in the Southern Sangre De Cristo Mountains and in Walsenburg in Huerfano county.  One to three inches of snow fell on Monument Ridge, north of Colorado Springs, and in parts of the adjacent plains in southeast Colorado.  One fatality was attributed to this storm.  James Hall, 83, of Wetmore in Custer county, was found Christmas Eve after apparently falling  outside of his home and dying of exposure.

A "southeaster" brought high winds to parts of Newport County where a peak gust to 63 mph was reported at Jamestown.  High wind gusts close to 60 mph also were reported from Charlestown and Middletown.  A peak wind gust to 55 mph was reported in Newport.  Strong southeast winds with gusts to 40 to 55 mph affected all of south coastal Rhode Island.  Scattered power outages were reported throughout the area with a total of 3,300 electric customers affected.  In Jamestown and Charlestown, where wind gusts reached close to 60 mph, boats were reported sunk and others broke loose from their moorings.  Many tree limbs and a few trees were reported blown down.  Sixteen foot waves were reported between Block Island and the mainland.  The effects of strong winds were felt inland as far north as the Providence area where a few trees and tree limbs were reported blown down, causing isolated power outages.  Up to two inches of rain fell with this storm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Summary of events of October 8, 1997:A line of severe thunderstorms developed and moved across western and central Oklahoma during the evening, producing large hail, damaging winds, and 2 tornadoes.  The first tornado was observed southeast of billings in Noble County.  No damage occurred, and the tornado was rated F0.  The second tornado touched down south of Coyle in Logan County, destroying a barn and some outbuildings.  Damage was rated F1.The largest hail (up to the size of golf balls) fell in Oklahoma City in Oklahoma County and in Addington in Jefferson County.  Severe thunderstorm wind gusts were estimated to be as high as 80 mph (in Perkins in Payne County).  Structural wind damage was reported west of White Eagle in Kay County, near Coyle in Payne County, and east of Guthrie in Logan County.  Tree damage was reported in Meridian in Logan County, south of Perkins and in Chandler in Lincoln County, in Edmond in Oklahoma County, east of Elgin in Comanche County, and in Marlow in Stephens County.See preceding individual Storm Data entries for further details and additional reports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lightning struck and set fire to a rural Chandler home.  Damage was estimated at $20,000.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another supercell thunderstorm, from radar indications, probably spawned a tornado in the Purgatoire River Valley north of U.S. Highway 160 15 to 20 miles east northeast of Trinidad.  The area the storm passed through is uninhabited, with no roads, and little vegetation to point out a tornado track.  However, gusty winds to 66 mph were measured on the rear flank of the storm south of the probable tornado.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous cars and homes had their windows broken.  One farmer lost over 100 acres of cotton as the hail knocked the cotton off of the plants and the heavy rains washed the cotton away. Other farmers lost crops as well.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The same supercell thunderstorm that brought large hail and a brief tornado to eastern Otero county produced a long track tornado through northwestern Bent and central Kiowa counties.  The tornado began about 7 miles west of Las Animas.  Eleven people were in the direct path of the tornado as it hit a ranch house and adjacent outbuildings.  Five men were caught outside, trying to move their vehicles from harm's way.   Four were thrown about by the tornado and received minor injuries.  Six women in the ranch house were unhurt.  The tornado moved northeast and blew a vehicle off Highway 194.  The occupant received minor injuries.  It destroyed a stream level monitor on the other side of the highway, then ripped through a line of trees before moving into barren country.  Eyewitnesses said the tornado remained intact for most of the 35 mile track northeast to just south of Highway 96 in Kiowa county.  Owing to the nearly uninhabited, barren landscape, little if any damage occurred beyond Highway 194 in Bent county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm system moved into Colorado from the west, bringing an abundance of moisture and gusty winds from 20 to 40 mph. The storm brought accumulations of 12 to 20 inches to the Eastern San Juan and La Garita mountains during the morning and afternoon of the 27th. The San Luis valley received 6 to 18 inches of snow the afternoon and evening of the 27th. The system then moved east and brought heavy snow to the Sangre de Cristo mountains and adjacent foothills and plains the evening of the 27th into the night of the 28th. A band of intense snowfall lasted for many hours over the Wet mountains, Wet Mountain Valley, southern Sangre de Cristo mountains, and Walsenburg area.  Total accumulations in those areas ranged from around 30 inches in the Wet Mountain Valley, around three feet in the southern Sangre de Cristo mountains and La Veta Pass, and at Walsenburg, Rye, and Beulah, to 45 inches at the 9,000 foot level in the Wet Mountains.  Nearly 30 inches of snow fell near Divide in Teller county.  Eight to 10 inches fell along the Palmer Divide, with generally less than 5 inches in the Colorado Springs area.  Pueblo tallied about 5 inches. The severe winter conditions closed numerous roads and highways, including Interstate 25 from Pueblo south to the New Mexico state line. Four thousand homes were without power in Pueblo West and Turkey Creek in Pueblo county when strong winds and heavy wet snow brought down hundreds of power poles. Ninety-two year old Marie Brandenburg of Westcliffe in Custer county died when she accidently locked herself out of her house, then slipped and fell by her back porch.  She froze to death in the high winds and heavy snow.

In Walkersville (Frederick Co), a deteriorating, aging silo on a local farm began tipping over the previous night, and winds on the 2nd brought it down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A considerably weakened Hurricane Nora was barely a tropical storm by the time its remnants reached southern Nevada.  It still managed to produce over an inch of rain in many southern Nevada locations even though the core of the storm tracked across Arizona.  The drenching only produced minor street flooding in Las Vegas and the Pahrump Valley.  Access to some outlying homes in Pahrump was cut off as flooded dirt roads became impassable.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large gravity-feed wagon was tipped over and damaged, several trees in a nearby shelter belt were uprooted, hay bales were rolled, unravelled and strewn over 1/2 mile and about 700 feet of fence and trees were damaged.  Two small unsecured sheds were rolled onto their sides.  Within a mile of this damage site at a nearby farm, a roof of a large outbuilding was partially removed, an untied trailer home was rolled over by the wind and damaged.  Approximately, 600 to 1000 acres of sunflowers were flattened and power lines were downed.

High winds knocked over a tree onto a building at a car dealership in Pierre.  Some of the automobile windows in the car lot were broken by blowing debris.  High winds also damaged a porch and skirting attached to a mobile home in Ft. Pierre and flattened the frame of a body shop that was under construction.
A tractor trailer was blown off interstate 29 just east of Watertown.

A strong cold front moving across the Great Lakes region collided with warm, moist, and unstable air across the southern Lower Peninsula on Friday afternoon, September 19, 1997. Thunderstorms developed ahead of the cold front. One mini supercell formed over Lake Michigan shortly after Noon EDT, then moved across Ottawa and Kent Counties before dissipating. The supercell produced hail up to 1 1/2" in diameter and yielded many reports of a rotating wall cloud, however no funnel clouds were reported. Later in the afternoon, a line of severe thunderstorms moved across southwest and south central Lower Michigan, producing wind gusts to 70 mph and small hail. Trees and power lines were downed in a line from Allegan County east-southeast through Jackson County. Around 10,000 customers in this swath lost power, nearly half of which occurred in Jackson County.

Record setting rains producing extensive flooding occurred from October 9-13, 1997 across portions of the South Texas Coastal Bend.  A high pressure area across the eastern U.S. and Gulf of Mexico combined with an area of low pressure from northern Mexico to force an influx of very moist and unstable tropical air into the Texas coastal plains.  Residual moisture from once Hurricane Pauline over the southwest Mexican Pacific coast also contributed to the tropical moisture feed.  A series of weak upper level disturbances interacted with the deep tropical airmass to produce numerous "training" bands of showers and thunderstorms across the Texas coastal plains from October 9-12.  During the early part of the event, a low-level inverted trough was analyzed across the Coastal Bend of South Texas.  An upper level area of high pressure had built across the area resulting in very light steering winds aloft.  Strong easterly winds with a long fetch across the Gulf of Mexico resulted in the threat of coastal flooding throughout the period.  Low level winds increased and veered to more of a southerly direction late on the 11th into the 12th in advance of a cold front pushing into the Central Plains.  This resulted in a great reduction in the precipitation across the area on the 12th with no flooding observed.  However, convergence ahead of the front late on the 12th and into the early morning hours of the 13th resulted in a redevelopment of numerous showers and thunderstorms across the area along with widespread flooding.  The Storm Total estimates from the WSR-88D at Corpus Christi, TX, as well as reports from observers, indicated rainfall totals ranging from 8 to 22 inches.  The greatest flooding occurred in the Corpus Christi area of Nueces county with an estimated $5 million in flood damages.  Unfortunately, two teenage brothers (ages 14 and 13) drowned after being swept away by flood waters while playing near a drainage basin in Annaville, TX (near Corpus Christi) in Nueces county.  The majority of the agricultural crops had already been harvested so damage to crops was minimal.  There were literally hundreds of automobiles stranded during the flood event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On Saturday, August 16, 1997, a cold front moved slowly south across Michigan's Lower Peninsula. One low pressure wave moved along the front early that morning, resulting in severe thunderstorm development over south central Lower Michigan. Later that afternoon, with very humid and unstable air in place across far southern Lower Michigan, another frontal wave caused severe thunderstorm development along the southern 2 tier of counties across southern Michigan. The thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall amounts of 2 to 5 inches in the counties bordering northern Indiana and northern Ohio, along with isolated reports of wind damage from 60 mph thunderstorm wind gusts. One thunderstorm produced golfball-sized hail in Edwardsburg in Cass County on Saturday afternoon. Local utility companies reported approximately 55,000 power outages during the afternoon and evening across far southern Michigan, most a result of lightning strikes, but some due to downed trees and utility poles.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minor tree damage reported, with limbs strewn along portions of U.S. Highway 12.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Iowa Gov. Terry Branstad requested disaster aid for 52 counties after an early season snowstorm dumped several inches of snow across the state.  Numerous traffic accidents were reported across the area with at least 2  serious accidents and several ditched vehicles. In Buchanan County several minor injuries were reported when a  bus went off Highway 20. One woman in Cedar Rapids was treated for injuries after she was struck by a falling tree branch.  Heavy snow downed power lines and trees and left about 120,000 persons without power across the area.  Rural Washington County residents were without 911 and long distance telephone service much of the day.  The storm closed the Cedar Rapids Airport stranding travellers for 5 hours.

A powerful Pacific storm brought high winds to the Oregon coast. The highest wind speeds reported included sustained winds of 55 mph with gusts to 89 mph at Florence in Lane county, sustained 60 mph with gusts to 80 mph at Tillamook in Tillamook county, sustained 60 mph gusting to 80 mph at Netarts in Clatsop county, and sustained 51 mph gusting to 80 mph in Newport in Lincoln county.

An intensifying low pressure system moved eastward across northern New England into the Gulf of Maine and caused strong northwest winds over most of the state on Thanksgiving Day.  High winds were reported at several places in the eastern part of the state.  A peak gust to 71 mph was recorded atop Blue Hill in Milton, while Falmouth Airport on Cape Cod has a gust to 69 mph.  In Middlesex County, a spotter in  Littleton reported a gust to 67 mph.  Wind gusts to 40 to 55 mph were common across the rest of the state.  Some gusts included:  Goshen, 53 mph; Worcester, 52 mph; Martha's Vineyard, 49 mph; Chatham, 48 mph; Nantucket, 47 mph; and Boston, 46 mph.  In Gloucester, the strong winds knocked a chimney off a house and some copper flashing off a downtown building.  No injuries were reported.  The strong winds knocked down tree limbs and wires and resulted in power outages affecting more than 4,000 electric customers across the state.

About an inch of rain fell within 20 minutes resulting in areas of street flooding.  A canal was unable to contain the high runoff and resulted in flooding of a business area with muddy water 2 to 3 feet deep.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Okemos Police Department reported 3/4 inch diameter hail in Okemos.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very wet snow fell in all of North Central, Northeast and East Central Kansas.  The precipitation was mostly snow from the onset in North Central Kansas.  In East Central and most of Northeast Kansas however heavy rain turned to heavy snow with snowfall rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour shortly after the changeover occurred.  Total accumulations were held down due to soaked ground and temperatures slightly above freezing.  The greatest snowfall of 4 to 6 inches fell generally north of Interstate 70.  Some specific amounts include Blaine and Concordia 6 inches, Circleville and Munden 5 inches,  Seneca 4 to 6 inches, Hiawatha, Marysville and Manhattan 4 inches.  Several vehicle accidents resulted with one of them fatal.  A motorist lost control on northbound US Highway 59 four miles north of Ottawa in Franklin County and was hit on the passenger side by a suburban vehicle as he slid into the opposing lane.  The motorist was killed while the driver of the suburban vehicle suffered minor injuries.

The storm intensified as it moved southeast from north of Palmer dropping large hail along its path.  The area from western Nance and Merrick counties south to western Clay county sustained the most damage.  The storm then blew through extreme southern Nebraska with winds in excess of 60 mph dropping limbs and power poles in Thayer county.

Intense low pressure moved into central Canada During the early morning hours of the 13th.  A strong cold front swept through Iowa as the low lifted north.  High winds swept in as the cold air overspread the state.  Sustained winds of 30 to 40 MPH were common with frequent gusts to between 50 to 60 MPH.  Scattered damage was reported over the west half of the state.  The only significant reports came from the north central counties, specifically Humboldt County.  Winds were recorded at 81 MPH near Rutland at 0347 CST.  These winds caused damage around $47,000 to a greenhouse there.  Thirty thousand dollars damage was to plants and produce.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Jasper county 911 reported golfball size hail on highways 83 and 11 near Adgateville. The hail was 3 inches deep in some areas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably dry weather and below normal rainfall, which became worse during the unseasonably warm summer months, caused an estimated $135,000,000 dollars in crop losses throughout the state of Maryland.  Hardest hit among the eastern shore counties was Kent where 70 to 75 percent of all crops were lost.  The corn harvest was 48 percent below 1996's level and yielded only 33.8 million bushels or about 75 bushels per acre.  The soybean harvest was about 25 percent below 1996's level and yielded only 13.3 million bushels.  During the month of August Secretary of Agriculture Dan Glickman declared the state of Maryland a primary disaster area.  This made farmers eligible for low interest loans.On July 17th,  the Susquehanna River Basin Commission issued a drought watch for the Susquehanna River Basin.   The commission expected this watch to continue through at least November.  Yearly precipitation totals through October 31st on a county weighted average were below normal in all of the Maryland Eastern Shore Counties,  with the greatest deficits in Kent (-6.0 inches)  and Cecil (-7.1 inches) Counties.  Yearly totals farther south were skewed by the heavy rain that fell on August 20th.  In the upper Eastern Shore Counties, the yearly precipitation totals were only about 80 percent of normal.

A strong coastal low pressure system moved northeast into southeastern Massachusetts from south of Long Island and brought high winds to many parts of southeastern Massachusetts, including Cape Cod and the Islands.  There were even a few gusts to hurricane force.  The strong winds blew from the east and southeast and gusts frequently reached 50 to 65 mph across much of the state...from Middlesex and Norfolk Counties east and southeast. Peak wind gusts of 81 mph were recorded both at Cuttyhunk Island west of Martha's Vineyard and atop Blue Hill in Milton.  Some of the other highest wind gusts reported included: 79 mph at the New Bedford Hurricane Barrier; 77 mph at Dennis; 73 mph at Hyannis; 71 mph at Marstons Mills (Falmouth); and 60 mph at Chatham.  Numerous trees and tree limbs were blown down, knocking out electrical power.  Outages affected up to 32,000 electric customers statewide, including 12,000 in southeastern Massachusetts and 20,000 in the Merrimack Valley.  There were scattered reports of trees falling onto homes causing scattered property damage.Heavy rainfall occurred, with the maximum totals of 2.0 to 3.6 inches reported from the south coast across Cape Cod and the Islands.  Heavy rain also fell across the rest of the state with 1.5 to more than 3.0 inches in less than 12 hours.  In Hampshire County, Worthington reported a total of 3.06 inches.    Lowell had 2.24 inches and Worcester had 2.22 inches.   In New Bedford, along the south coast, 3.47 inches was reported.  Major urban street flooding occurred in Dartmouth, New Bedford, and Acushnet.  There were many reports of flooding...and not just in poor drainage areas.  There were reports of minor shore road flooding along the south coast and along Martha's Vineyard's shores at normally vulnerable locations.  Thirteen crewmen had to be rescued from a sinking fishing vessel off of Gloucester.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A vigorous Pacific Storm moved across southern Nevada dumping significant snow in the mountains during a 12 hour period.  In the Spring Mountains, the 8500 foot level of Lee Canyon received nine inches of snow and seven inches fell at the 7000 foot level in Kyle Canyon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure moving norteastward from the mid-Atlantic coast brought the first significant snowfall of the season to parts of southern and central New Hampshire.  Snowfall amounts ranged from 6 to 10 inches in southern and central areas with 2 to 4 inches in Coos County.  Much of the precipitation in coastal areas fell as sleet.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed in eastern Oklahoma during the early morning of November 5th and produced large hail. Quarter size hail fell at Talala, Porter, and just south of Kiowa, and dime to quarter size hail fell at White Oak. Dime to nickel size hail fell at numerous other locations in eastern Oklahoma.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong southeast winds associated with a deep low pressure center over the Great Lakes knocked down trees and power lines in the southern part of the state, especially in coastal areas.  More than 40,000 customers lost electrical service in the affected areas, some for several days.  Several boats were damaged or destroyed when they broke loose from their moorings and were swept onto rocks.

A cold front moved across western Lower Michigan during the early morning hours of November 12th, resulting in a lake-enhanced snow event which began late evening, Tuesday, November 11th. In general, 1 to 5 inches of snow fell across western and southern Lower Michigan, with 3 to 5 inch amounts confined to Lake, Ottawa, Kent, Allegan, Barry, Eaton, Ingham, and Kalamazoo Counties. The snow-covered and icy roads caught many overnight and early morning motorists by surprise. Slippery conditions are believed to have contributed to a seven-car pile-up on the northbound span of the U.S. 31 drawbridge late Tuesday night in Grand Haven. Two injuries were reported. The snow initially melted on road surfaces overnight, then froze early Wednesday morning as temperatures fell below freezing. This resulted in extremely icy conditions and an unusually high number of minor accidents, which included many slide-offs into ditches. Accidents with injuries were reported in Battle Creek, St. Joseph and Cass Counties, Hillsdale County (a rollover accident), and  Branch, Mecosta, Osceola, and Newaygo Counties. Snow reports included 5.0 inches in Grandville, 4.8 inches at the National Weather Service Office in southeast Grand Rapids, 4.5 inches in Hudsonville, 3.6-4.0 inches in Allegan, 3.2 inches in Hastings, 3.0 inches in Oshtemo, 3.0 inches in East Lansing, and 1.5 inches in Battle Creek.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: F1 tornado damaged approximately 12 homes.  Numerous trees and power lines down.  A van was overturned by high winds.  Both occupants suffered minor injuries.
Severe thunderstorm winds downed trees along Georgia Highway 41 near Brooksvile.  Minor flooding reported.
Severe thunderstorm winds downed power lines with several outages reported in Bronwood and Dawson.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Gradient winds caused widespread damage to trees and property in Iowa and Illinois.  Over 65,000 power customers were without power for several days due to downed power lines. A large cottonwood tree fell on a home in Camanche causing serious structural damage.  The winds slowed river operations at Lock and Dam 13 near Fulton IL as some boaters were afraid to leave the safety of the narrow channel and enter the wide open upstream pool where winds might capsize their boats.

A strong coastal low pressure system moved northeast into southeastern Massachusetts from south of Long Island and brought high winds to many parts of southeastern Massachusetts, including Cape Cod and the Islands.  There were even a few gusts to hurricane force.  The strong winds blew from the east and southeast and gusts frequently reached 50 to 65 mph across much of the state...from Middlesex and Norfolk Counties east and southeast. Peak wind gusts of 81 mph were recorded both at Cuttyhunk Island west of Martha's Vineyard and atop Blue Hill in Milton.  Some of the other highest wind gusts reported included: 79 mph at the New Bedford Hurricane Barrier; 77 mph at Dennis; 73 mph at Hyannis; 71 mph at Marstons Mills (Falmouth); and 60 mph at Chatham.  Numerous trees and tree limbs were blown down, knocking out electrical power.  Outages affected up to 32,000 electric customers statewide, including 12,000 in southeastern Massachusetts and 20,000 in the Merrimack Valley.  There were scattered reports of trees falling onto homes causing scattered property damage.Heavy rainfall occurred, with the maximum totals of 2.0 to 3.6 inches reported from the south coast across Cape Cod and the Islands.  Heavy rain also fell across the rest of the state with 1.5 to more than 3.0 inches in less than 12 hours.  In Hampshire County, Worthington reported a total of 3.06 inches.    Lowell had 2.24 inches and Worcester had 2.22 inches.   In New Bedford, along the south coast, 3.47 inches was reported.  Major urban street flooding occurred in Dartmouth, New Bedford, and Acushnet.  There were many reports of flooding...and not just in poor drainage areas.  There were reports of minor shore road flooding along the south coast and along Martha's Vineyard's shores at normally vulnerable locations.  Thirteen crewmen had to be rescued from a sinking fishing vessel off of Gloucester.

An intensifying low pressure system moved eastward across northern New England into the Gulf of Maine and caused strong northwest winds over most of the state on Thanksgiving Day.  High winds were reported at several places in the eastern part of the state.  A peak gust to 71 mph was recorded atop Blue Hill in Milton, while Falmouth Airport on Cape Cod has a gust to 69 mph.  In Middlesex County, a spotter in  Littleton reported a gust to 67 mph.  Wind gusts to 40 to 55 mph were common across the rest of the state.  Some gusts included:  Goshen, 53 mph; Worcester, 52 mph; Martha's Vineyard, 49 mph; Chatham, 48 mph; Nantucket, 47 mph; and Boston, 46 mph.  In Gloucester, the strong winds knocked a chimney off a house and some copper flashing off a downtown building.  No injuries were reported.  The strong winds knocked down tree limbs and wires and resulted in power outages affecting more than 4,000 electric customers across the state.

Record setting rains producing extensive flooding occurred from October 9-13, 1997 across portions of the South Texas Coastal Bend.  A high pressure area across the eastern U.S. and Gulf of Mexico combined with an area of low pressure from northern Mexico to force an influx of very moist and unstable tropical air into the Texas coastal plains.  Residual moisture from once Hurricane Pauline over the southwest Mexican Pacific coast also contributed to the tropical moisture feed.  A series of weak upper level disturbances interacted with the deep tropical airmass to produce numerous "training" bands of showers and thunderstorms across the Texas coastal plains from October 9-12.  During the early part of the event, a low-level inverted trough was analyzed across the Coastal Bend of South Texas.  An upper level area of high pressure had built across the area resulting in very light steering winds aloft.  Strong easterly winds with a long fetch across the Gulf of Mexico resulted in the threat of coastal flooding throughout the period.  Low level winds increased and veered to more of a southerly direction late on the 11th into the 12th in advance of a cold front pushing into the Central Plains.  This resulted in a great reduction in the precipitation across the area on the 12th with no flooding observed.  However, convergence ahead of the front late on the 12th and into the early morning hours of the 13th resulted in a redevelopment of numerous showers and thunderstorms across the area along with widespread flooding.  The Storm Total estimates from the WSR-88D at Corpus Christi, TX, as well as reports from observers, indicated rainfall totals ranging from 8 to 22 inches.  The greatest flooding occurred in the Corpus Christi area of Nueces county with an estimated $5 million in flood damages.  Unfortunately, two teenage brothers (ages 14 and 13) drowned after being swept away by flood waters while playing near a drainage basin in Annaville, TX (near Corpus Christi) in Nueces county.  The majority of the agricultural crops had already been harvested so damage to crops was minimal.  There were literally hundreds of automobiles stranded during the flood event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous reports of flooding and closed roads.

Measured winds gusted to around 60 mph in parts of Colorado Springs.  In Florence, in Fremont county, around 11:30 a.m., a tree fell on a 100-year old house causing heavy damage. A few trees were uprooted and scattered power outages were reported around the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong and moist Pacific trough produced 6 to 12 inches of snow in most mountain areas of western Colorado.  Heavier totals included 17 inches at Purgatory Ski Area, 14 inches at Rio Grande Reservoir,  14 inches at Crested Butte, 13 inches at Red Mountain Pass, and 13 inches at Snowmass Ski Area, Additionally, strong winds produced areas of blowing and drifting snow.  Some peak wind gusts at mountain top locations included 82 mph at Telluride and 66 MPH at Snowmass.

The snow began around 5 pm on Nov 9 and lasted into the evening of Nov 11.  Snow totals included Trimountain (10 SW of Houghton) 18.5 inches, Marquette County Airport 18 inches,  Phoenix (25 NE of Houghton) 16 inches, Redridge (10 W of Houghton) 14 inches and Eben (15 SW of Munising) 11 inches.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Boulder City Police Department reported flood waters had closed Georgia Street and Riviera Court and Buchanan and Broadmore.  Also, an 11 year old boy was caught in a drainage ditch by flood waters and had to be rescued.  The exact time was unknown.  He escaped with only minor injuries.  The flood waters also damaged the Georgia Avenue drainage channel and washed away dirt fill which set back repair efforts to roads from a recent flash flood event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heavy rains on the Bookcliff Mountains raised the water level by 6 feet in Government Creek and sent 1 to 2 feet of water roaring into the western side of Rifle.  Some businesses and about a dozen homes received flood damage.  In the aftermath, rocks, mud, and other debris had to be removed from roads and lawns.

Several fast moving,, short lines of thunderstorms packing severe winds pushed east through many south-central Wisconsin counties and blew over large trees or broke large tree limbs out of trees.  Some power lines were also pulled down by the broken limbs.  In Shullsburg, (Lafayette Co) a 20 by 40 foot building caved in and a small shed was destroyed.  A chicken house was blown down near Monticello in Green county. About 11000 customers lost power due to the downed power lines or other lightning strikes.  Four different homes were struck by lightning in Muskego (Waukesha Co).  One home had fire damage to its roof and gable, while the other three experienced minor fires and smoke damage.  Elsewhere, lightning struck a lakeshore guest home on Browns Lake (Racine Co) east of Burlington, resulting in severe fire damage.  Lightning also struck a home on the shore of Bohner's Lake south of Burlington, resulting in a minor roof fire.  Lightning was also busy in the city of Fond du Lac (Fond du Lac Co)  where it struck two different transformers within an hour, leaving 3722 custormers without electricity.

On Saturday, August 16, 1997, a cold front moved slowly south across Michigan's Lower Peninsula. One low pressure wave moved along the front early that morning, resulting in severe thunderstorm development over south central Lower Michigan. Later that afternoon, with very humid and unstable air in place across far southern Lower Michigan, another frontal wave caused severe thunderstorm development along the southern 2 tier of counties across southern Michigan. The thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall amounts of 2 to 5 inches in the counties bordering northern Indiana and northern Ohio, along with isolated reports of wind damage from 60 mph thunderstorm wind gusts. One thunderstorm produced golfball-sized hail in Edwardsburg in Cass County on Saturday afternoon. Local utility companies reported approximately 55,000 power outages during the afternoon and evening across far southern Michigan, most a result of lightning strikes, but some due to downed trees and utility poles.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds stripped the tops off 3-4 mature maple trees and 5 cottages along East Long Lake received minor damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A "southeaster" brought strong east to southeast winds to coastal eastern Massachusetts with wind gusts to 40 to 55 mph.  Tree limbs and a few trees were reported blown down, especially over Cape Cod and the Islands and across south coastal towns in Plymouth and Bristol County.  In New Bedford, a tree fell on a house and car.  In Dartmouth, a staging was toppled at the University of Massachusetts.  At least five boats washed ashore and countless others lost rudders at Mattapoisett Harbor.  The town wharf was under about six inches of water at high tide.  The harbormaster rated this storm as one of the top five bad storms during recent years.  Minor coastal flooding was reported at many points along south facing coastlines of southeastern Massachusetts, with tides one to two feet above normal.  The strong winds in the Boston area reached sustained speeds of 30 mph at Deer Island in Boston Harbor.  A peak gust to 51 mph was recorded from the east-southeast at the Blue Hill Observatory in Milton at 11:08 AM.  Heavy rain accompanied the winds.  Very heavy rain fell on Martha's Vineyard where the storm total was 3.8 inches.  This was the same storm system that hit Atlantic City, NJ with a deluge of around 14 inches of rainfall.

Strong low pressure over the upper Great lakes brought strong winds to northern Illinois during the afternoon of Monday September 29. The winds peaked between 200pm and 400 pm CDT (1300-1500CST) Some peak wind gusts included; Morris, Grundy County 64 mph, Peru, La Salle County 58 mph, Watseka, Iroquois County 56 mph, Carol Stream, DuPage County 53 mph, Aurora, Kane County 52 mph, NWS forecast office in Romeoville, Will County 49 mph, Palwaukee Airport, Wheeling and O'Hare Airport, Chicago, both in Cook County 47 mph,  Woodstock, Mc Henry County 47 mph, and Rockford Airport, Winnebago County 45 mph.  The wind died down during the evening. The strong winds blew down numerous tree limbs and a few large trees throughout northern Illinois. The falling limbs knocked out power to over 40,000 customers. Flights were delayed at O'Hare Airport. A tree fell on a police car in Barrington Hills, but the officer in the car was not injured. The high winds also fanned brush and grass fires in Livingston, Ford and Iroquois Counties.

Evening thunderstorms produced strong winds, heavy rain, and lightning across central and northeast Wisconsin.  Three inches of rain fell near Wausau (Marathon co.) and Marshfield (Wood co.) in only two hours, resulting in basement flooding.  Thunderstorm winds ripped shingles off a house and knocked down several trees in Knowlton (Marathon co.).  The storm moved east and blew trees and a power pole down in Shawano county.  Yet another storm in the town of Marion (Waushara co.) produced strong winds which toppled a tree onto a corn crib, crushing it, and leaving a mass of trunk, limbs and foliage.Lightning also produced damage during the evening.  A barn was set ablaze by lightning in the town of Neva (Langlade co.).  Near Green Bay (Brown co.), a tractor, which had been left idling in low gear, was struck by lightning, which caused it to start moving on its own.  The tractor meandered through a corn field before it "burned to a crisp."

Severe thunderstorms rolled across the area during the evening hours producing damaging winds estimated at sixty to seventy miles per hour. The winds downed trees and power lines and resulted in thousands being left without  power. In Cheektowaga, the wall and roof of a large cinder block building were blown down.
Heavy rains brought a flash flood which washed out a section of County Road 102.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy thunderstorm rain caused small stream flooding and flooding at St. Rts. 7 and 82 at Brookfield Center, where two feet of water covered the road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A "southeaster" brought high winds to parts of Newport County where a peak gust to 63 mph was reported at Jamestown.  High wind gusts close to 60 mph also were reported from Charlestown and Middletown.  A peak wind gust to 55 mph was reported in Newport.  Strong southeast winds with gusts to 40 to 55 mph affected all of south coastal Rhode Island.  Scattered power outages were reported throughout the area with a total of 3,300 electric customers affected.  In Jamestown and Charlestown, where wind gusts reached close to 60 mph, boats were reported sunk and others broke loose from their moorings.  Many tree limbs and a few trees were reported blown down.  Sixteen foot waves were reported between Block Island and the mainland.  The effects of strong winds were felt inland as far north as the Providence area where a few trees and tree limbs were reported blown down, causing isolated power outages.  Up to two inches of rain fell with this storm.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: 2 pivot sprinklers overturned...power poles blown down...a small airplane hanger was destroyed...a combine was rolled and crumpled up.
3 inch tree limbs blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The dry spell that existed the last 10 days of August continued through the first three weeks of September, especially over the south half of the state. Little or no rain fell in the south while one storm system produced scattered thunderstorms in the north half of the state on the 10th. University of Georgia agricultural experts estimated crop losses statewide at $66.5 million.

Peak sustained winds were 40 mph on Whidbey Island.  Oak Harbor had winds gusting to near 60 mph.  About 5000 customers in Western Washington lost power at some time during the day.  There were a few reports of  trees down and blocking roadways.

A moderate low intensified to 967mbs and moved east northeast to near  Dutch Harbor  Saturday morning.  The low then drifted east and began to slowly weaken.  Winds preceding the front with this low were southeasterly and gusted up to 46 mph.  Behind the low...winds gusted close to 60 mph across the Aleutians.

A vigorous cold front moved through New Jersey during the early morning on the 27th and was accompanied by strong gusty winds.  The strongest gusts occurred during two surges,  one within a couple of hours of the cold frontal passage.  The second (and in most areas just as strong) surge occurred during the late morning on the 27th.  At about 1120 a.m. EST, a 31-year-old woman was killed when she was struck in the head by a falling tree limb and knocked off her horse during a fox hunt on the Ellisdale Road property of Princeton Nurseries in Upper Freehold Township in Monmouth County.  The strong winds pulled down tree limbs and this resulted in power outages to about 20,000 homes throughout the northern half of New Jersey.  Some of the hardest hit areas included Newton (Sussex County) and Flemington (Hunterdon County).  Peak wind gusts included 55 mph in Harvey Cedars (Ocean County)  and at the McGuire AFB (Burlington County) and 53 mph in Belmar (Monmouth County) and Chatham (Morris County).  While it was also windy in the southern third of New Jersey, the highest wind gusts were a bit lower, generally between 35 mph and 45 mph.

A slow moving nor'easter caused strong winds, beach erosion and widespread, but minor, tidal flooding from mid-day on the 7th through the afternoon on the 8th.  The low pressure system formed near Cape Hatteras on the morning of the 7th and moved slowly north as the surface low was captured by a closed low at higher levels of the atmosphere.  On the morning of the 8th,  it was located about 80 miles east of Wallops Island Virginia and on the morning of the 9th,  it was near Cape May City.  That morning a second low pressure system was located near Cape Cod Massachusetts and the two merged into one and was located just south of Nova Scotia by the morning of the 10th.  The low came close enough to the New Jersey shore by the morning of the 9th to cause the onshore winds and consequently the tidal flooding to diminish.The several tide cycle pounding cause beach erosion along the New Jersey Coast and it became severe in a few locations.  In Cape May County, in Sea Isle City, severe erosion occurred from 89th through 93rd Streets and the ocean came within 15 feet of the Tiburon Shores Condominiums.  The surf removed dunes and steps in that area.  In Ocean County, in Harvey Cedars, the pounding surf scoured a six foot cliff north of Bergen Avenue.  In Brant Beach, waves crashed close to the dunes on  41st Street.  In Monmouth County, the surf removed about 50 to 100 feet of beach in Manasquan and created a four foot cliff in Spring Lake. The persistent onshore flow raised tidal departures to 3.0 to 3.5 feet above normal and around 2.5 feet above normal at times of high tide from mid-day on the 7th (Friday) through the afternoon on the 8th (Saturday).  This caused widespread, but minor,  tidal flooding from the mid-day high tide on the 7th through the afternoon on the 8th.   The highest tides reported were 6.6 feet above mean low water in Atlantic City, 6.9 feet above mean low water in Sandy Hook and 7.4 feet above mean low water in Cape May City.  In Monmouth County, tidal flooding was reported along the Shrewsbury River in Rumson and Sea Bright.  In Ocean County, in Beach Haven, minor tidal flooding occurred along Bay Avenue and minor flooding was also reported in Barnegat.  In Atlantic County, in Absecon, the intersection of  U.S. Route 9 and Shore Road were closed for several hours the evening of the 7th.  Some bayside blocks in southern Atlantic City were flooded.  In Cape May County, tidal flooding forced the closure of several blocks in Ocean City and Wildwood. Strong gusty winds buffeted the region from the morning of the 7th through the afternoon of the 8th.  The strongest gusts were reported during the afternoon and evening of the 7th.  Peak gusts included 59 mph in Williamstown (Gloucester County), 56 mph in Seaside Park and Harvey Cedars (both Ocean County), 47 mph at the Marina in Atlantic City, 45 mph in Belmar and 44 mph in Wildwood.  In Ocean County, the strong winds caused power outages to about 5,000 homes in Stafford Township and ripped away beach fencing in Beach Haven.  During the same storm, a ship reported a severe thunderstorm that produced wind gusts to 86 mph at 10 p.m. EST on the 8th about 100 nautical miles east of Cape May County.

Remains of ex-typhoon David moved just south of Amchitka (in the central Aleutians) late Saturday.   A second system was "ejected" northwestward into the Gulf of Alaska in advance of this system.  Winds in the Gulf of Alaska adjacent to the central North Gulf Coast reached speeds close to 45 mph.  Ahead of the low that was once Typhoon David, wind gusts reached close to 45 mph...however much stronger western winds gusting close to 60 mph were observed on the "back" side of the low.  Brisk northwest winds continued for  a stretch in the eastern Aleutians well after the ex-typhoon moved to some 450 miles south of Kodiak Monday.

A strong cold front moving across the Great Lakes region collided with warm, moist, and unstable air across the southern Lower Peninsula on Friday afternoon, September 19, 1997. Thunderstorms developed ahead of the cold front. One mini supercell formed over Lake Michigan shortly after Noon EDT, then moved across Ottawa and Kent Counties before dissipating. The supercell produced hail up to 1 1/2" in diameter and yielded many reports of a rotating wall cloud, however no funnel clouds were reported. Later in the afternoon, a line of severe thunderstorms moved across southwest and south central Lower Michigan, producing wind gusts to 70 mph and small hail. Trees and power lines were downed in a line from Allegan County east-southeast through Jackson County. Around 10,000 customers in this swath lost power, nearly half of which occurred in Jackson County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained National Weather Service spotter reported 4-6 inch diameter tree limbs were knocked down by thunderstorm winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably warm weather returned to the Milwaukee metro area during the overnight hours ending on the morning of the 12th.  Milwaukee's overnight low of 61 was a new record high minimum reading.

Low pressure moving norteastward from the mid-Atlantic coast brought the first significant snowfall of the season to parts of southern and central New Hampshire.  Snowfall amounts ranged from 6 to 10 inches in southern and central areas with 2 to 4 inches in Coos County.  Much of the precipitation in coastal areas fell as sleet.

A very strong winter weather storm and blizzard moved across the central plains states through the day Saturday.  The 74 year old female from Adams Oklahoma was returning home when her car became stuck in a snowdrift less than a mile from her home.  She apparently died from hypothermia after trying to walk through the blizzard from her stranded car to her nearby home.  She was found about noon the next day under about eighteen inches of snow in a milo field southeast of Hooker.   Reports from the Oklahoma Mesonet sites in both Cimarron and Texas counties indicated wind gusts of 58 to 66 mph from 0830 CST to 1700 CST.  Total snowfall accumulations across the Oklahoma Panhandle Saturday were from four to twelve inches across Cimarron and Texas counties and two to six inches across Beaver county.  There was also an indirect death which occurred two weeks after the winter storm and blizzard.  A man died from injuries sustained in a multicar accident.  The accident occurred on a closed road and those involved in the accident had gone around a barricade.  Most roads in the Oklahoma Panhandle were closed during the winter storm and blizzard.  There were numerous multicar pile ups with many churches and gyms full of stranded motorists.  About 12,000 to 15,000 head of cattle were lost in this storm mainly in Texas county, but also Cimarron and Beaver counties.  The high winds produced snow drifts of three to five feet.

An elderly women died from environmental cold-weather hypothermia based on medical reports.  She was found dead on her home's driveway.  Outside temperatures during the morning were in the mid to upper 30s.  One can speculate that she slipped and fell on the driveway and was unable to get up.

A very strong winter weather storm moved across the central plains states through the day Saturday.
